opus-5.5.text:
I think evaluations are going to become one of the central pillars of AI governance, and the field is still very immature relative to the weight we're going to put on it.

Right now a lot of evaluation work is a kind of craft. Talented people sit down, think hard about what a dangerous capability might look like, say in cyber offense or biology or persuasion, and design tasks to probe for it. That's valuable, but it's not yet a science. We need to move toward something more like a mature measurement discipline, where we understand what our evaluations are actually measuring, how reliably, and how results generalize to the real world.

A few things I think need to develop. First, **validity**. When a model passes or fails a benchmark, what does that tell us about its behavior in deployment, or about what a motivated actor could get out of it with scaffolding, fine-tuning, or lots of attempts? We often don't know. Elicitation is a big part of this: if you don't try hard enough to bring out a capability, you'll underestimate it, and the gap between what a lab finds in a week and what the whole world finds over a year can be large.

Second, **anticipation**. Capabilities are advancing quickly, and evaluations tend to saturate. We need evaluations that tell us not just whether a model can do something today, but give early warning about what's coming in the next generation, so we have time to put safeguards in place before the capability arrives.

Third, evaluating **propensities and not just capabilities**. As systems become more agentic, the question isn't only "can it do X?" but "would it do X, and under what circumstances?" That's harder to measure, and it raises questions like whether a model behaves differently when it suspects it's being tested.

Fourth, the **institutional ecosystem**. Evaluations matter most when they feed into decisions: deployment choices, safety frameworks, regulation. That requires shared standards, independent third-party evaluators with real access, and ways for governments and the public to trust results without everything being taken on a developer's word. The AI safety institutes and the growing evaluation community are a promising start, but we need much more capacity and much more rigor.

So my overall view is that evaluation should become a field in its own right, with the scientific depth and institutional infrastructure that we have for, say, testing in aviation or pharmaceuticals, adapted to a technology that changes much faster and is far more general than those.

r001.rationale: The response compares evaluation to aviation and pharmaceutical testing, but does not compare its required contextual understanding to psychology or sociology.

r002.rationale: It describes current task design and calls for more rigorous measurement, but does not argue that open-ended exploration should complement formal, prespecified evaluations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think evaluation is really one of the load-bearing pieces of the whole governance picture, and it's still quite immature relative to the weight we're asking it to carry. Almost every policy proposal you hear — responsible scaling policies, if-then commitments, licensing regimes, international agreements — bottoms out in some claim like "we'll be able to tell when a model crosses a threshold of dangerous capability." And right now our ability to actually tell that is much weaker than those proposals implicitly assume.

So the first thing I'd say is that evaluation needs to become a proper science, with the things that implies. Right now it's more like a craft. A lot of what we do is: a clever team sits down, thinks about what a dangerous capability might look like, builds a benchmark, runs it, and reports a number. That's valuable, but it has a few well-known problems. One is elicitation — if the model scores low, is that because it lacks the capability, or because we didn't prompt it well, didn't fine-tune it, didn't give it the right tools or scaffolding? We've seen repeatedly that capabilities that looked absent turn out to be present once someone finds the right way to ask. So a negative result on an eval is much weaker evidence than it looks, and we need a much better theory of how close our elicitation efforts are to the frontier of what a motivated actor could extract.

The second problem is validity — does the thing we're measuring actually track the thing we care about? We care about, say, whether a model could meaningfully uplift someone trying to build a biological weapon, or whether it could autonomously replicate and acquire resources, or whether it's being deceptive about its own goals. Those are complex, real-world, multi-step phenomena, and our evals are necessarily proxies. The gap between the proxy and the underlying construct is something we mostly hand-wave about, whereas in a mature field — think of psychometrics, or clinical trials — there's an enormous apparatus around construct validity, predictive validity, calibration against ground truth. We need that apparatus.

Third, and this gets more to the governance side, I think evaluation needs to develop as an institution and not just as a technique. Who runs the evals? Who sees the results? What happens when a model fails one? At the moment most of this is done inside the labs, which is natural because that's where the expertise and the model access are, but it creates obvious problems of incentive and credibility. The model developer is also the entity that most wants the model to pass. So I'm quite keen on the development of third-party evaluation capacity — things like the AI Safety Institutes, independent organisations like METR or Apollo — with real access, real resources, and some institutional independence. And over time I'd like to see that evolve toward something closer to what we have in other high-stakes domains: standardised protocols, accreditation, a degree of adversarial scrutiny, and ideally some international coordination so that a model evaluated in one jurisdiction has results that are legible and trusted elsewhere.

And then there's a layer beyond capability evals that I think is underdeveloped, which is evaluating propensities and dispositions rather than capabilities. Can the model do X is one question; will it do X, under what conditions, and can we trust its own reports about that? That's where you get into things like evaluations for deception, sandbagging, situational awareness — whether the model knows it's being tested and behaves differently. This is genuinely hard, because a sufficiently capable system that wanted to pass an eval could in principle do so, and so you need either interpretability tools that look inside rather than just at behaviour, or evaluation designs that are robust to the model gaming them. We don't have that yet, and I think it's one of the most important open problems.

The last thing I'd emphasise is that evaluation needs to be forward-looking, not just a snapshot. The interesting question for a decision-maker often isn't "what can this model do today?" but "what will the next model be able to do, and how much warning will we get?" So we need to pair evals with scaling trends, with forecasting, with some notion of safety margins — the idea that you set your thresholds conservatively enough that you have time to act after you cross them, rather than discovering you're past the line. That connects to the broader governance challenge: the point of evals is to inform decisions, and so the field has to develop in dialogue with the people making those decisions, so that the outputs are actually actionable and not just interesting.

So in short: more science, more independence, more attention to propensities and not just capabilities, and a tighter coupling to the actual decisions they're meant to support. I'm reasonably optimistic that the field is moving in that direction, but the pace at which it needs to mature is quite demanding given how fast the models are improving.

r001.rationale: The response compares evaluation to psychometrics and clinical trials around validity and calibration, but does not compare it to psychology or sociology in the depth of contextual understanding required.

r002.rationale: It discusses formal science, standardised protocols, and adversarial scrutiny, but does not say that open-ended exploration of model behavior should complement prespecified evaluations.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to move from thinking of evaluation as a score on a benchmark to thinking of it as a science of understanding what these systems can do, and under what conditions. A model might perform poorly when you ask it a question directly, but perform much better when it has tools, more time, or a different way of breaking down the problem. So the object we’re evaluating is often a whole system, rather than just a model.

And there’s an important asymmetry here. If you demonstrate that a system can do something dangerous, that’s useful evidence. If you fail to get it to do that thing, it’s much harder to know what you’ve established. Is the capability absent, or did you just not find the right way to elicit it? We need evaluations that are explicit about that uncertainty.

I’d also want the field to become much more connected to decisions. What result would lead you to delay deployment, restrict access, or require additional safeguards? You want to work that out before you see the results, rather than negotiating what a concerning result means after the fact.

So there’s a technical research agenda, but also an institutional one: developing independent expertise, giving evaluators sufficient access, and making sure their findings can actually inform consequential decisions. The aim shouldn’t be a certificate that says ‘safe’. It should be a much better basis for deciding which risks we’re prepared to take.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a science of understanding systems and their conditions, but does not compare this depth of contextual understanding to psychology or sociology.

r002.rationale: It contrasts benchmark scores with broader system understanding and calls for prespecifying how results inform decisions, but does not clearly say open-ended exploration should complement formal, prespecified evaluations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to move from thinking of evaluation as a benchmark score to thinking of it as a science of understanding what these systems can do, and under what conditions they might do something dangerous.

There are at least two distinct questions here. One is about capabilities: could a model help someone carry out a cyberattack, or accelerate some dangerous biological work? The other is about behaviour: when would it actually provide that assistance, or take harmful actions itself? A system might have a capability that doesn’t show up with a particular prompt, but does show up when you give it tools, more time, or a different kind of scaffolding. So a negative result can be quite difficult to interpret.

That means we need much more investment in the methodology: how you elicit capabilities, how you know your tests are measuring what you care about, and how you communicate uncertainty. We also need independent evaluators who have sufficient access to the models and the expertise to really investigate them.

And then evaluations need to connect to decisions. What finding would cause you to delay a deployment, add safeguards, or restrict access? If we haven’t worked that out, we can produce lots of interesting measurements without actually improving safety. Ideally, we build an ecosystem where evaluations are continually challenged and updated, and where their results have consequences for how systems are developed and deployed.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a science of understanding model capabilities and behavior, but does not compare evaluation to psychology or sociology or communicate that similar depth of contextual understanding is required.

r002.rationale: The response supports continual challenge and updating of evaluations, but does not say that open-ended exploration should complement formal, prespecified evaluations.
